White-throated nightjars (Eurostopodus mystacalis) are medium-sized, cryptic caprimulgids inhabiting coastal forests and woodlands of eastern Australia. Adult females, which are slightly larger and more heavily marked than males, achieve a maximum recorded body mass of approximately 160 grams [Wwi = approximately 160 grams], while adult males attain an ultimate wet weight of about 124 grams [Wwi = about 124 grams], figures derived from extensive museum specimen series and field measurements. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females averaging roughly 29% heavier, is thought to relate to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. Early developmental studies, drawing on comparative data from the congeneric European nightjar Caprimulgus europaeus, estimate that hatchlings emerge at a wet weight at birth of around 13.5 grams [Wwb = around 13.5 grams]. This neonatal mass represents a relatively small proportion of adult weight, consistent with the altricial mode of development typical of the Caprimulgidae, wherein chicks are brooded intensively and provisioned by both parents from the moment of hatching.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, measured at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], hatchlings exhibit an incubation period lasting approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days] before emergence from the shell. This age at birth, derived from field observations of monitored nests, falls within the 22- to 28-day range documented for other nightjar species and appears tightly linked to the thermal regime of the incubating adult. The extended incubation reflects the relatively low basal metabolic demands of the developing embryo. Once hatched, the nestling phase proceeds rapidly, with the developing chick achieving first flight and parental independence at roughly 31 days after hatching [tx = roughly 31 days after hatching] at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This fledging period is relatively compressed for a bird of this adult size, perhaps an adaptation to minimise predation risk in ground-nesting species that rely on cryptic plumage and immobility for concealment.

Sexual maturation in the White-throated nightjar proceeds along a predictable developmental schedule. Under the same thermal conditions approximating core body temperature (39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]), young individuals attain gonadal maturity and the onset of reproductive potential approximately 93 days after birth [tp = approximately 93 days after birth]. This relatively rapid progression to puberty, occurring within a single breeding season for birds hatched early in the spring, is notable among caprimulgids and may reflect the constraints of a seasonally unpredictable insect food supply. Despite attaining sexual maturity relatively quickly, first breeding is typically deferred to the following austral spring. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 2.1 years since birth [tR = approximately 2.1 years since birth], a delay that likely reflects the need for young birds to acquire foraging proficiency, establish a breeding territory, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the demands of egg formation and noctur at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]nal incubation.

Reproductive output in this species is notably constrained. Under the body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a characteristic shared with many other nightjar species, and typically produce just one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. This exceptionally low fecundity, among the lowest recorded for any Australasian bird, is partially offset by a comparatively extended lifespan; at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at approximately 15.1 years [am = approximately 15.1 years], a figure derived from long-term banding studies of marked individuals. This longevity, combined with the deferred onset of reproduction, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises adult survival and repeated breeding attempts over high annual reproductive output, a pattern consistent with other tropical and subtropical caprimulgids facing unpredictable environmental conditions.

Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from respirometry trials conducted under standardised laboratory conditions, at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], indicate a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 86.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 86.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, when corrected for body mass, placed the White-throated nightjar within the expected range for caprimulgids, a group known for relatively low metabolic rates compared to other birds of similar size. The combination of low fecundity, prolonged lifespan, and modest metabolic expenditure appears well suited to a foraging niche that relies on aerial insectivory during crepuscular periods, where prey availability can be sporadic and energetically costly to pursue. Such life-history trade-offs underscore the species’ adaptation to the unpredictable food resources of its sclerophyll forest habitat and highlight the conservation implications of any further disruption to its foraging or breeding grounds.
